title: Bill 44 repeals the Alberta Sheriffs Police Service's Crown-corporation status and moves staff under the Public Service Act
summary: Introduced on November 23, 2026 under Premier Danielle Smith as a 163-page First Reading omnibus bill (168-page PDF amending 20 provincial statutes), Section 12 of Bill 44 repeals the Police Act's 2025 Crown-corporation structure (s. 33.4(2)) and the Bill 15 employee-transfer chapters (Parts 3.3 and 3.4). It establishes the Alberta Sheriffs Police Service directly as a non-corporate statutory force whose employees are appointed under the Public Service Act, shifts municipal service contracts under s. 33.75 to the Crown in right of Alberta, and provides a three-year transitional wind-down window for the existing corporation (s. 33.951).
attribution: Legislative Assembly of Alberta, Bill 44 (First Reading, Nov. 23, 2026), s. 12

title: Bill 44 repeals mandatory public fatality inquiries for custodial deaths, shifts next-of-kin report access to regulation, and omits a transitional clause
summary: Section 6 of Bill 44 repeals Fatality Inquiries Act s. 33(3)—codified in 2005 (PC era) and narrowed in 2017 (Notley NDP, SA 2017 c 8 s 2) only to carve out youth deaths already reviewed by the Child and Youth Advocate (s. 33(3.1)-(3.2)) while keeping adult peace-officer and correctional custody inquiries mandatory unless due solely to natural, unpreventable causes or unrelated to care. In its place, the Board applies unpublished Cabinet-prescribed factors (ss. 33(2), 55(e)) with no statutory duty to publish reasons when declining an inquiry. Section 6 also downgrades next-of-kin medical-examiner report access to discretionary under regulation (s. 30(2)), adds compulsory addiction facilities to medical-examiner notification only (s. 12(1)(a)), and contains no transitional savings clause for pending inquiries.

title: Four-province statutory baseline: ON and QC house police under ministries, while BC, MB, and ON mandate custodial inquests
summary: Verified primary statutes across four Canadian provinces distinguish policing structure from custodial-death inquests. On policing, Ontario's Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019 (s. 2(1)) employs OPP officers under Ontario's Public Service Act and Quebec's Police Act (s. 50) places the Sûreté du Québec under the Minister of Public Security—both non-corporate ministry models. On custodial deaths, however, British Columbia (Coroners Act, s. 18(2)-(2.1)), Manitoba (The Fatality Inquiries Act, s. 19(5)), and Ontario (Coroners Act, s. 10(4)) all mandate public inquests for custodial or peace-officer force deaths (with BC obligating published reasons whenever waived), whereas Quebec pairs discretionary inquests (Coroners Act, ss. 104-106) with mandatory independent BEI police-death investigations (Police Act, ss. 289.1-289.2).
attribution: ON CSPA 2019 & Coroners Act; QC Police Act & Coroners Act; BC Coroners Act; MB Fatality Inquiries Act

title: Alberta Next Panel advised against a policing referendum despite 52% polling opposition, and the October 19, 2026 ballot omitted RCMP replacement
summary: In December 2025, the government-appointed Alberta Next Panel recommended transitioning community policing from the RCMP to an Alberta Police Service prior to the 2032 contract expiry without holding a referendum—arguing that over 80% of Albertans already receive policing from municipal services or Alberta Sheriffs—even though its own report recorded 52% opposition in professional polling (44%, 41%, and 48% support across three 2025 waves, lowest of seven measures) and majority opposition in online surveys. Cabinet's Orders in Council 109/2026, 110/2026, and 160/2026 set ten questions for the October 19, 2026 stand-alone referendum with zero questions on RCMP replacement.

title: Separate bases: 2021 PwC forecast (~$366M transition, $735M-$759M/yr) vs. 2026-2031 municipal cost-share ramp (22% to 30%)
summary: Two distinct non-summable financial baselines frame Alberta's policing debate. Under Premier Jason Kenney, the October 2021 PwC Transition Study forecast roughly $366M over six years in transition costs (about $241M operating and $125M capital) and $735M to $759M in annual operating costs for a full provincial police force, alongside roughly $170M per year in federal RCMP cost-sharing (30% under PPSA; 30% or 10% under MPSAs). Separately, under Premier Danielle Smith, the Renewed Police Funding Model effective April 1, 2026 increases rural and small-municipality shares of actual frontline PPSA costs from 22% in 2026-27 by two percentage points annually to 30% in 2030-31+, while adding a Vacancy Modifier and Population Density Subsidy.
